title: The $1.9 trillion private credit vehicle total masks differences in loan exposure, leverage and liquidity
bank: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
summary: U.S.-domiciled private credit vehicles held about $1.9 trillion in assets at year-end 2025, roughly eight times their $240 billion in 2012. Federal Reserve researchers use the newly published Financial Accounts aggregates to show why that headline is a poor proxy for either outstanding private loans or the risk borne by a particular fund investor. Vehicles can hold equities and debt securities alongside loans. They can borrow from banks, lock up investors’ capital for years, or offer limited opportunities for investors to withdraw. A privately negotiated loan can consequently sit beneath very different claims on the cash flows it generates (sections 2–3 and figures 1–2).

The authors define private credit according to how financing reaches the borrower. The instrument is privately negotiated and financed principally through a nonbank investment vehicle. The perimeter includes direct lending to middle-market companies as well as loans secured on real estate, infrastructure, equipment and other assets. It excludes loans or privately placed securities held directly by banks, insurers and other institutions. Borrowers can still use a private term loan alongside a bank revolver. The domestic figure measures the assets of vehicles domiciled in the United States. A footnote separately identifies $763 billion held by foreign-domiciled vehicles that invest in the United States.

Private debt funds were the largest segment, at about $940 billion. Business development companies held $570 billion, interval and tender offer funds $290 billion, and middle-market collateralized loan obligations $50 billion. Total vehicle assets grew 21% between 2024 and 2025, with BDC assets up 30% and interval and tender offer funds up 39%. Yet private loans were only 57% of private debt fund assets, compared with nearly 80% at BDCs and 26% at interval and tender offer funds. Corporate equities accounted for 44% of the last group’s assets. Middle-market CLOs hold loans and give investors different priority claims through their tranches. Growth in vehicle assets therefore cannot be read directly as new lending to companies (figures 2–5).

Funding creates a second source of divergence. Private debt funds had about $234 billion of debt in 2025, almost two-thirds supplied by domestic banks. Average debt relative to net asset value was around 0.25, while the 90th percentile was near one. BDCs carried about $260 billion in debt, financed mainly by banks, with corporate bonds also important. Their average leverage was about one and the upper decile threshold about 1.5. Interval and tender offer funds borrowed about $21 billion, some 90% from banks, but averaged a debt-to-NAV ratio of only 0.05. Rising debt in dollars can thus coexist with relatively stable leverage ratios. Banks retain exposure as fund creditors even when the underlying borrower receives financing outside a bank’s loan book (figures 6–8).

Investor withdrawal terms explain part of the portfolio differences. Private debt fund investors typically commit capital and lack an early redemption right. Listed BDC shareholders can sell on an exchange, whereas perpetual non-traded BDCs often offer limited repurchases subject to board discretion. Interval funds must offer periodic repurchases, commonly 5% of shares per quarter. Tender offer funds can choose whether and when to make an offer. The need for cash and the applicable leverage limits help explain why vehicles with direct access for individuals may hold substantially different portfolios (section 4).

Measurement is least direct for private debt funds. SEC Form PF does not label them as a distinct type, and detailed positions are available for only a subset. The authors combine strategy information, fund names and external classifications, then impute missing holdings using comparable strategies. The private debt fund estimates exclude uncalled commitments. These are estimates of funded portfolios at reporting dates. They cannot by themselves reveal loan-level losses, changes in valuation practices, or the cash available to meet a particular vehicle’s next repurchase offer (data appendix and figure A1).

questions.question: Where could investor repurchases force a sale of illiquid assets?
questions.detail: The note distinguishes mandatory interval offers from discretionary tenders and non-traded BDC repurchases. It gives no vehicle-level cash forecast. Examine shareholder reports, prospectuses, tender filings and N-PORT holdings for cash, liquid securities, actual tenders, proration and upcoming maturities. Match these against scheduled offers and loan repayments. This would identify which vehicles can meet cash demands while retaining their private loan portfolios.

questions.question: How concentrated is the link to bank balance sheets?
questions.detail: Banks are major creditors to all three fund categories with reported borrowing, but aggregate balances do not show bank-by-bank exposure or drawdown risk. Use BDC credit agreements and public filings, bank credit disclosures and regulatory lending data where available to trace borrowers, undrawn commitments and covenants. Common lenders could reduce liquidity across several funds at once, affecting exposure beyond any one bank or fund allocation.

questions.question: How much portfolio risk changes when imputed private debt fund holdings are replaced with measured holdings?
questions.detail: The appendix explains its classification and imputation, while the leverage distribution shows some smaller funds borrow heavily. Seek the authors’ classification checks, Form PF reporting definitions and audited fund statements for comparable strategies. Compare asset composition and leverage within strategy and by size. That test would indicate whether average exposures are adequate inputs for portfolio stress analysis or whether the tails require separate treatment.
